transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-13
Time: 10:00 AM PST
Duration: 45 mins
Attendees: Samira Patel (AE), Marcus Li (SE), Jordan Kim (CSM) - Redwood; Priya Rao (Head of ML), Carlos Mendes (Platform Eng), Liam O'Connor (CTO) - NexaHealth

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check audio ok?
[00:03] Priya: Yep loud and clear, thanks Samira.
[00:06] Samira: Cool. Agenda Marcus will walk the benchmark slides, then we'll do tuning suggestions and close with next steps. Jordan will capture follow-ups.
[00:12] Marcus: Alright, I pulled the latest bench results from the spreadsheet you all shared, link in the doc drive.google.com/open?id=bench-xxxx. I ran Redwood hosted with batch=4, kv-cache off, int8 quant on for the smaller model, and compared to your baseline cluster which is running fp16 on their custom infra.
[00:28] Carlos: Just to be clear, baseline was the in-house cluster with T4s and 8 workers, right?
[00:31] Marcus: Yes that's correct, T4 cluster with custom sharding.
[00:34] Priya: Ok good. We're most concerned about p95 and p99 tail latency our SLAs are user-facing so spikes matter.
[00:40] Marcus: Understood. Quick high-level: p50 latency on Redwood hosted is 120ms vs baseline 140ms; p95 is 420ms vs baseline 280ms; p99 is 1,200ms vs baseline 620ms. Throughput wise, baseline sustains slightly higher steady-state RPS at same cost profile due to aggressive batching. But they hit higher tail latencies.
[00:58] Liam: Hmm that's interesting baseline cheaper per-token but tail is worse or better?
[01:02] Marcus: Baseline better p95/p99? sorry to clarify: baseline shows better p50 and p95 in this config due to bigger batch sizes, but tail p99 gets worse on Redwood in this specific hosted config because of our autoscaling cold-starts and smaller batch defaults. There's some noise in today's run, likely from the test pattern.
[01:20] Priya: We saw earlier notes about cold starts. How many cold starts in this run?
[01:24] Marcus: Roughly 2-3 cold start events during the 30-minute window; that inflated the p99. If we pin instances (Dedicated) or increase min-instances, that goes away.
[01:32] Samira: Also remember we had prefix/KV cache off in the run. Enabling it reduces per-token compute and should help both latency and throughput for repeated prefixes.
[01:40] Carlos: Right our workload is chatty, many similar prompts, so prefix cache should help a lot.
[01:44] Marcus: I did a quick simulated run enabling KV cache and increasing batch to 8 on a testbed: p50 100ms, p95 260ms, p99 520ms, throughput +18%. Those were on a small testbed, not full production.
[02:00] Priya: That's promising did you notice quality regression with int8 quant?
[02:04] Marcus: For the Llama-variant we used, int8 showed minimal regressions on our eval set (BLEU-style metrics and a couple of prompt-based checks). We'll share the eval diffs. But if you need strict parity, we can test int8 with dequantization fallbacks or use bf16 on Dedicated.
[02:18] Liam: Cost wise, how does hosted int8 compare to our baseline fp16?
[02:22] Marcus: Roughly comparable token cost at current rates; Redwood hosted with int8 plus caching reduces effective token compute by ~25-30% in repeated patterns. Baseline is cheaper if they run huge batches, but remember user-visible latency may suffer.
[02:36] Priya: Can you walk through the test parameters? Sequence length distribution?
[02:39] Marcus: Sure we used the sample traces you provided: p50 seq len 120 tokens, p95 480, p99 1024. Request interarrival had a 60/40 split between short sessions and longer ones. We can take more accurate traces if you provide them.
[02:53] Priya: We'll send updated traces with true traffic spikes. Carlos will attach them.
[02:57] Carlos: Yep I'll upload two traces to the shared folder after the call.
[03:00] Marcus: Great. A few tuning notes: 1) Enable KV/prefix cache big wins if you have repeated contexts. 2) Increase batch size to 8 or 16 for throughput-bound requests but cap for latency-sensitive routes. 3) Use int8 quantization where acceptable; fallback to bf16 for critical routes. 4) Consider Dedicated to avoid cold-start noise and pin min instances.
[03:23] Samira: On Dedicated vs hosted tradeoff Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and predictable tail latencies, but it's a committed cost. Hosted is flexible and quicker to iterate.
[03:32] Liam: For our SREs, predictable latency is critical. We'd likely look at Dedicated for the production rollout, but want to understand how much more cost.
[03:39] Samira: We can run a TCO estimate I'll include cost-by-expected-RPS in the spreadsheet.
[03:44] Priya: Security question is Redwood's hosted environment SOC2 compliant? We need SOC2 + SSO/SAML and KMS integration for key management.
[03:51] Jordan: Yes, Redwood maintains SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, and KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments. We'll send the whitepaper and SOC2 report; for Hosted we can provide audit logs.
[04:04] Carlos: For Private/VPC deployment, what's the timeline? We have procurement constraints and need on-prem options for some silos.
[04:11] Samira: Private deployment timelines vary for VPC it's typically 4-6 weeks, on-prem can be longer depending on gating. We'll schedule a technical deep-dive to scope that.
[04:20] Marcus: Back to benchmarks I noticed one noisy run where autoscale spun up new instances causing 2s spikes. If you pin min-instances to 2 and enable warm pools, p99 drops substantially.
[04:32] Priya: Any suggestions for probing production-like load without disturbing our users?
[04:36] Marcus: Use the replay traces against a dedicated test environment. We can mirror traffic and run a soak test. Also we'll use our differential testing harness to compare outputs and latency.
[04:46] Liam: On quality, you mentioned eval diffs. Can we get side-by-side comparisons for the top 50 prompts?
[04:50] Marcus: Yes, we'll package the eval diffs and sample outputs for the 50 prompts. Expect them in the shared folder.
[04:57] Priya: One more competitors. If we end up using Anthropic or OpenAI, they offer low tail latency but locked-in APIs. We want portability. How easy to switch models with Redwood?
[05:06] Samira: Redwood supports model cataloging and model variants; switching is a config change and can be rolled out gradually with canaries. We also support fallback policies to a cheaper model if one variant is unavailable.
[05:16] Marcus: Quick recap of tuning experiments I propose: run quantized int8 + KV cache + batch 8 on a full 1-hour soak; run pinned min-instances test; capture p50/p95/p99 and throughput. We'll also run a quality check on the outputs.
[05:30] Priya: Sounds good. Anything else?
[05:33] Jordan: I'll create the next sync for next Friday same time and include infra.
[05:36] Carlos: I'll upload the traces and also our deployment constraints doc.
[05:40] Samira: Great. Recap of next steps: Samira sends security docs and updated cost sheet; Marcus runs the two experiments and shares logs; Priya/Carlos provide traces; Jordan schedules follow-up.
[05:52] Liam: Thanks everyone, that's helpful.
[05:54] Samira: Thanks all, see you next week.

End of transcript.
